items.q: What is meant by **"enterprise"**, **"resource"** and **"planning"**?
items.answer:
**Enterprise** — an organization providing a set of products or services to society; **a business entity**, from mid-size companies to huge conglomerates with multi-crore/billion sales. *Examples: Airtel, Tatas, Birlas, Mahindras, Reliance, IBM, Google, Apple.* An enterprise is **a group of people with a common goal**.

**Resource** — what the enterprise deploys: **human resource, machines, plants, storehouses, material stock**.

**Planning** — what it must decide in advance: **production, forecasts, money, new products, logistics, maintenance**.

Read together: **an organisation deciding in advance how to deploy what it has.**

items.q: Give a **definition of ERP**.
items.answer:
**Textbook definition:** *ERP is an **integrated information system** built on a **centralized database** and having a **common computing platform** that helps in **effective usage of enterprise's resources** and facilitates the **flow of information between all business functions** of the enterprise **(and with external stakeholders)**.*

The five bolded phrases each carry marks — and the final clause about **external stakeholders** is the one most often dropped. It is what **Extended ERP / ERP II** later formalises.

**Gartner's alternative** is worth adding for contrast, because it opens with *"is a **business strategy**"* — making the point that ERP is not a software purchase but a decision about how the business will operate.

items.q: What were the **four major drivers** of the ERP revolution in the last four decades?
items.answer:
**Remember them as EPIC** — each is a *from → to* shift:

| | Driver |
|---|---|
| **E** | **From department to enterprise** |
| **P** | **From function to processes** |
| **I** | **From information silos to integrated information system** |
| **C** | **From departmental database to company-wide integrated database** |

**If asked to *explain* rather than list**, give the chain — each driver is the precondition for the next:

You cannot manage at **enterprise** level without seeing whole **processes**; you cannot see a whole process without an **integrated system**; and an integrated system is only possible on a **common database**.

*Marks are lost for stating only the destination — always give both halves of each shift.*

items.q: What is the difference between the **department view** and the **enterprise view** of the organisation? / How is a **process approach** different from a **functional approach**?
items.answer:
**Department (functional) view** — the organisation is a set of specialised units, each with its own objectives, employees, software, database and reports. Each is measured on **its own targets**.

**Enterprise (process) view** — the organisation is a set of **end-to-end business processes** that cross departments and deliver value to a customer.

| Functional | Process-oriented |
|---|---|
| Department-focused | **Customer-focused** |
| Separate databases | **Shared database** |
| **Local** optimization | **Enterprise** optimization |
| Manual communication | Automated workflow |
| Data duplication | **Single source of truth** |
| Slow decision making | Real-time decision making |
| Limited visibility | **End-to-end visibility** |

**The clinching argument:** the customer only ever experiences the **process** — they never experience your org chart. Optimising the org chart optimises something no customer can see.

**The classic failure:** *Production → Quantity, Sales → Variety.* Both departments hit their targets while the enterprise loses — Production makes 50,000 units, Sales can only sell 30,000.

items.q: What are the **three major challenges of information silos**? How is an integrated information system better?
items.answer:
**The three challenges — mnemonic DNS:**
1. **D**uplication of data
2. **N**o integration between the departmental databases
3. **S**ystems not able to update all relevant information online

**Why the integrated system is better** — the three stated advantages of a company-wide database:
- **No data duplication**
- **Data standardization**
- **Data tracking**

These arrive in order and each enables the next: **one copy** makes **one format** possible, which makes **full history tracking** possible — and tracking is what makes **compliance and auditing** feasible.

**Concrete illustration:** Nestlé USA paid **29 different prices for vanilla to the same vendor**, and ran **nine different general ledgers with 28 points of customer entry** — a pure information-silo failure.

items.q: Explain the **disadvantages of individual departmental informal systems**.
items.answer:
**The enterprise scenario:** purchase-department information is **not available or compatible** with Production's needs, and **does not link to Finance or HR**. A variety of systems creates **IT maintenance nightmares** and **duplication of data and processing infrastructure** — *vendor details stored in multiple systems*. The result: **optimal planning is difficult without integration**, and the estate is **hard to change** because of compatibility issues.

**The ten problems of disintegrated data:** duplicate data entry · data inconsistency · poor communication · delayed information sharing · reduced productivity · increased operational costs · manual reconciliation · difficulty in decision-making · difficulty in compliance and auditing · reduced customer satisfaction.

**Remember them as a chain rather than a list:**

*Duplicate entry → inconsistency → manual reconciliation → delay → bad decisions → unhappy customers.*

**Also note the cascading effect:** a delay in one function hits another — *a design delay in R&D hits product shipment in Logistics.*

items.q: What is **MRP**? How do MRP systems work and what fundamental problem do they solve? How is **closed-loop MRP** different?
items.answer:
**MRP = Material Requirement Planning** (1960–70s). It works **backwards from the production schedule and the bill of materials** to compute what parts are needed, in what quantity, and by when — solving the manufacturer's fundamental problem of **having the right materials, in the right quantity, at the right time**, computed rather than guessed. Its stated benefit was **inventory and process time reduction**.

**Closed-loop MRP — the difference:**

> The MRP plan generated **does not consider the feasibility of the plan**, since it **does not consider the capacity available while planning**. In closed-loop MRP the plan is **validated, compared with reality and checked for feasibility**, and **alerts and triggers are reported to the planner** to take appropriate steps if issues are found.

**Why plain MRP produces impossible plans:** it can correctly conclude *"to ship 1,000 laptops on the 30th, order 1,000 processors on the 5th"* while saying nothing about whether the factory can **build** 1,000 laptops that month. **MRP assumes infinite capacity.**

**One line: MRP plans as if capacity were unlimited; closed-loop MRP checks the plan against real capacity and raises alerts.**

items.q: What is **MRP II**? What additional processes does it include over MRP?
items.answer:
**MRP II = Manufacturing Resource Planning** (1980s). Note **both** words change from MRP — *Material → Manufacturing*, *Requirement → Resource* — reflecting the widening from *what parts do I need* to *what resources does the whole plant need*.

**Additional processes over MRP:**
- **Forecasting**
- **Sales and operations planning**
- **Integration with accounting and billing**

The deck's summary: *"MRP II addresses traditional gaps by incorporating forecasting, sales and operations planning etc."*, giving **greater reduction due to integration with accounting, billing**.

**Why it matters in the story:** MRP II is where the plan first acquires a **money dimension**. MRP could say what to buy; MRP II could say what it costs and whether you can afford it. **This is the first cross-functional integration in the whole history**, and it is the template for everything ERP later did.

items.q: What are the **ten business benefits** of an ERP system?
items.answer:
The deck lists twelve; name as many as you can:

1. **Brings best practices**
2. **Facilitates seamless integration**
3. **Facilitates inter- & intra-organization communication and collaboration**
4. **Provides real-time information**
5. **Support for BPR**
6. **Automates transaction-oriented processes**
7. **Brings superior data management and eliminates redundancy**
8. **Improves key processes** such as Quote to Cash and Order Fulfilment
9. **Improved customer service**
10. **Better flexibility**
11. **Better customer satisfaction**
12. **Better planning, analysis and decision making**

**Group them into four families to regenerate the list:** **Data** (real-time info, data management, no redundancy) · **Process** (integration, automation, Q2C, BPR) · **People** (communication & collaboration, best practices) · **Outcome** (customer service, satisfaction, flexibility, decision making).

**Add the caveat for full marks:** benefits are really **"co-benefits" of ERP + IT + Business Engineering**, though the distinct driving force is ERP — which is why ROI attribution is inherently approximate.

items.q: How does ERP **reduce cycle time** of operations? Illustrate with a business process.
items.answer:
ERP reduces cycle time because **the order is entered once and every department automatically receives the information relevant to its role** — replacing emails, spreadsheets and re-keying with a shared database and automated workflow.

**Illustrated on Quote to Cash (O2C):**

1. **Quote / Proposal** → Sales Quote
2. **Quote Approval** *(by the customer)* → Approved Quote
3. **Sales Order** → Sales Order
4. **Fulfillment / Delivery** → Goods Delivered
5. **Invoicing** → Customer Invoice
6. **Payment Receipt** → Payment Received
7. **Cash Application** → Cash Applied / Account Closed

**Without ERP**, each handover is a manual re-entry with a queue behind it; the availability check at step 3 may not happen at all, producing a **wrong promise**.

**Why Q2C matters:** **revenue** (faster processing → faster revenue), **customer satisfaction**, **cash flow**, **operational efficiency**, and **visibility** from quotation to payment.

*Note the cycle does not end at delivery — stages 5–7 are about **getting paid**, which is why "reducing days outstanding" is a named tangible benefit.*

items.q: What are the **three major categories of ERP challenges**? List the items under each.
items.answer:
**Mnemonic: "I See People" (I-S-P).**

**A) Implementation challenges (6):** Scope changes · Huge budget · Long timeline · Process redesign · Unrealistic expectation · Complex interfaces

**B) Support / maintenance challenges (6):** Getting the right people · Managing multiple vendors · Managing regular updates · Technology obsolescence · Large application portfolio · Realizing benefits

**C) Managing people challenges (4):** Managing change · Managing large project team · Managing employee retention and relocation · Top management support

**They map onto the life cycle:** **I** = phases 1–5, **S** = phase 6, **P** = across all of them.

**Two elaborations worth adding:**
- *"Many implementations driven **purely** by BPR have failed"* — the failure is one of **dosage**, taking on new software *and* new ways of working simultaneously.
- *"Resolve issues of co-operation amongst seniors"* — ERP forces department heads to give up autonomy, and only **top management** can compel that.

items.q: Explain the issues related to **ERP maintenance and support**.
items.answer:
**The six support/maintenance challenges:** getting the right people · managing multiple vendors · managing regular updates · technology obsolescence · large application portfolio · **realizing benefits**.

**Elaborations:**
- **Right people for the support job** — the implementation team holds knowledge that exists nowhere else, which is why handover is done in a **staggered manner** and the core team is often **extended for support**.
- **Vendor management for SLA** — support runs to a service-level agreement.
- **Upgrades** — of both the **ERP** and the **technology**, and *"can be difficult if too much customization was done during implementation"*, requiring **backup, roll back, regression testing and documentation upgrades**.
- **Maintaining synchronization with other enterprise app life cycles** — your ERP, CRM and SCM are upgraded by different vendors on different schedules, and upgrading one can break its interface to another.

**"Realizing benefits" is the entry worth highlighting:** benefits accrue **during operation**, not at go-live — after the project team has disbanded. This is why **business case tracking** at milestones is needed.

items.q: Explain some of the **emerging trends** in the ERP market.
items.answer:
**The ten trends:** stratification of products (SAP, Oracle & the rest) · mainline ERPs adding functions all the time · niche players under pressure · SME focus · verticalized features · new deployment models (**Cloud ERP**) · **maintenance itself as a sizeable service** · newer types of ERP projects (**migration, consolidation & harmonization, upgrades**) · **embedded AI** · **data, analytics and process intelligence**.

**Group them into four stories:**

| Story | Trends |
|---|---|
| **The market is consolidating** | stratification · mainline ERPs adding functions · niche players under pressure |
| **The market is broadening downward** | SME focus · verticalized features |
| **The delivery model is changing** | cloud ERP · maintenance as a service |
| **The work itself is changing** | new project types · embedded AI · analytics & process intelligence |

**Note that the first two pull in opposite directions and both are true:** the top of the market concentrates around SAP and Oracle while the bottom opens to smaller companies — **the middle gets squeezed**.

**Trend 8 has a cause:** most large enterprises already run an ERP, so growth is no longer in first-time implementations but in **changing the one you have**.

items.q: What is meant by the **ERP life cycle**? What are its phases?
items.answer:
**ERP Lifecycle = ERP Implementation Life cycle + ERP Support Life cycle.**

**The six phases in sequence** — *Papa Please Bring Rice For Supper*:

| # | Phase | Also called |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Pre-Implementation** | Evaluation phase |
| 2 | **Project Preparation** | — |
| 3 | **Business Blueprinting** | Design phase |
| 4 | **Realization** | Build phase |
| 5 | **Final Preparation and Go Live** | *(Fine Tune)* |
| 6 | **Support** | Manage phase *(Sustenance)* |

**Each phase has specific activities, deliverables and milestones.** Phases 1–5 are implementation; **phase 6 is support**, and it is half the life cycle rather than an epilogue.

**Why ERP gets its own life cycle:** adaptation **has a very high impact on business operations**, **needs top management commitment & support**, is **complicated and needs special focus**, requires **special teams** and **end user involvement**, and involves **many activities and stakeholders**.

items.q: Explain the critical **(a) activities, (b) typical deliverables and (c) milestones** of the **Pre-implementation** and **Project preparation** stages.
items.answer:
**PRE-IMPLEMENTATION**

*Activities:* team formation · **feasibility / ROI / business case** · budgeting · requirements collection and prioritization · **scope freezing** (typically at function/module level) · **partner / package selection**.

Two bodies are formed — the **steering committee** (senior, managerial) and the **implementation team** (technical, product expert). Requirements definition is *"very tricky, conflicting organization politics"*, sometimes needing consultants to resolve. The **RFP** is *"an intense activity"* where *"cost is not the only criterion"*.

*Deliverables:* **scope · high-level plan · selected team + partner + package · contract agreements · budget approvals · contracts drafted, finalized and approved.**

**PROJECT PREPARATION**

*Activities:* team selection (internal and external) · **detailed scope** · **create project mission/vision (charter)** · decide implementation methodology · standards/governance · technical preparation (**solution architecture, hardware sizing and configuration design**) · plan resources and schedules · **kick-off meeting** · orientation training to senior & key people.

*Deliverables:* **detailed plan · vision and mission statements · technical (software) design · hardware sizing & configurations · project plan · resource plan · training plan · project charter.** All must be **agreed by relevant stakeholders** for the milestone.

**The boundary between them:** *Pre-implementation chooses **whether and with whom**; Project preparation chooses **how**.* Pre-implementation ends before commitment — the organisation could still decide not to proceed.

items.q: Explain the critical **activities and deliverables** of the **Business Blueprinting** and **Realization** stages.
items.answer:
**BUSINESS BLUEPRINTING (Design)** — *"the key step of reviewing business processes and the upcoming ERP system."*

*Activities:* **model As-Is process** · detailed requirements (workshops, current problems, other initiatives) · **Business Process Re-engineering** · **To-Be process** · **gap analysis** · review/audit of blueprint · **core team training**.

*Deliverables:* **current model (As-Is) · detailed requirement · gap document · future To-Be process.**

The logic is **As-Is + To-Be ⇒ Gap**. The **gap document** is the most consequential deliverable in the life cycle, because every gap must either be **customized** or **absorbed by changing the business** — which is why *gap analysis is "the most important step of ERP implementation"*.

**REALIZATION (Build)** — *"the 'creation' of the new system"*; designing, building, testing and packaging for deployment.

*Activities:* **configuration** · **gap bridging developments / customization** · **unit + integration testing** · training plan for end users.

*Deliverables:* **configured/modified software with installation scripts · technical documentation on deployment and hardware configuring · quality check documentation · final functional/technical specifications · end user training material · data/system migration document.**

**Customization risks:** **stability** of base functionality · **deviating from best practice** · **maintainability**. Customize heavily and you forfeit *"brings best practices"* — benefit #1 — and make every future upgrade harder.

items.q: Explain the critical **activities and deliverables** of **Final Preparation & Go Live** and of **Support**.
items.answer:
**FINAL PREPARATION AND GO LIVE — the ten final checks:**

1. Stress / volume / system tests
2. **User acceptance**
3. **End user training**
4. **Data migration**
5. Set up **Help Desk** / resource teams
6. **Audit by external team**
7. **Communications to all stakeholders** — cut-over date, *"clearly specify what to expect and what not to"*, with agreement and commitment by all
8. **Contingency plans for the cut-over**
9. Hardware / network infrastructure availability
10. **Go / No-Go**

**At cut-over:** switch over to the new system · **execute parallel runs of the old system for a defined period** · Help Desk, hand-holding and escalation management · **typically done in phases/batches** · fine-tune configuration issues.

**Implementation closure:** closure meeting · **final acceptance sign-off** · create a small team to **"harvest"** knowledge, re-usable parts and marketing/branding materials.

**SUPPORT** — *"stabilization, fine tuning and look-ahead"*: **staggered handover** from implementation to support team · work on open issues · **execute support per SLA** · measure and improve performance · ensure **"business-class" operations** (reliability, availability, data backup) · develop hooks and interfaces to second-line applications · manage **upgrades** (backup, roll back, regression testing, documentation).

**Why parallel runs:** cut-over is the least reversible moment in the project. The parallel run is how you **detect** a wrong number, and how the business keeps running if the new system fails.

items.q: Why does an ERP implementation need a **methodology**? Who provides one? Give examples.
items.answer:
**Definition:** *a methodology is a set of rules, methods and tools to achieve a specific goal in a specific way* — a set of steps carried out in a particular sequence, with **proven activities, deliverables, templates and accelerators**, that provides **guidance, a framework and process check points**.

**Why one is needed:**
- **ERP adoption has equal emphasis on product and implementation**
- **Since the product is stable and "available", success solely depends on good implementation**
- **Implementation expert companies command a premium, hence!**

The argument in full: **everyone buys the same SAP**, so the software cannot be the differentiator — **how it is implemented** is. That is why methodologies carry brand names and why implementation firms charge a premium.

**Who provides them:** ERP vendors and consulting firms. **They were developed through 100s of implementation best practices** — distilled from experience, which is what the *harvest knowledge* step of closure feeds.

| Owner | Methodology |
|---|---|
| **SAP** | **ASAP** |
| **PwC / IBM** | **Ascendant** |
| **Oracle** | **AIM / Fast Forward** |
| **Scala / Epicor** | **Signature** |

items.q: What is **ASAP**? What are its objectives, phases and tools? What is **Ascendant**?
items.answer:
**ASAP = Accelerated SAP methodology Roadmap**, owned by **SAP**.

**Objectives** — *"Quick Managers Involve Process Reuse"*:
1. **Quick and cost effective implementation**
2. **Maximize resource utilization**
3. **Involve users community**
4. **Process oriented**
5. **Re-usability**

**Tools:**
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Roadmap composer** | assembles the phase-by-phase roadmap |
| **Q&A database** | structured requirement capture |
| **Project IMG** | **Implementation Guide** |
| **Transports** | **configuration move from dev to deployment** |
| **BC Sets** | **configuration recorder** |

*Transports and BC Sets are a pair: BC Sets **record** a configuration, Transports **carry** it to the live system — the practical basis of the re-usability objective.*

**ASCENDANT (PwC / IBM)** — an **integrated programme** covering six workstreams: **Project Management · Business · Organization · Application · Architecture · Operations**. **These span all the phases** — Evaluation → Project Preparation → Business blueprint → Realization → Final preparation → Go Live and support → Sustain.

**The key contrast:** **Ascendant is a grid, not a sequence.** Six workstreams run horizontally across seven phases, so the project is always doing all six concerns at once. **ASAP optimises for speed and reuse; Ascendant for coverage and continuity** — and Ascendant has an explicit **Organization** (change-management) stream that ASAP's objectives do not name.

items.q: Explain the **four common ERP deployment strategies** with the pros and cons of each.
items.answer:
**The grid — locations × modules:**

| Approach | **Locations** | **Modules** |
|---|---|---|
| **Big bang** | **All** | **All** |
| **Rollout** | Selected | All |
| **Big bang Modular** | **All** | Selected |
| **Rollout Modular** | Selected | Selected |

*Naming is regular: **Big Bang** = all locations, **Rollout** = selected locations, **Modular** = selected modules.*

**The five-parameter comparison:**

| Parameter | Big bang | Rollout | BB Modular | Rollout Modular |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Risk** | High | Average | High | **Low** |
| **Time** | **Low** | Average | Average | High |
| **Learning scope** | **Low** | High | Average | High |
| **Change mgmt** | High | Average | High | **Low** |
| **Resource demand** | High | Average | High | **Low** |

**The governing trade-off: risk and time move in opposite directions.** Big Bang is fastest and riskiest; Rollout Modular is slowest and safest. **Risk, change management and resource demand move together** — all three measure *how much is happening simultaneously*.

**The trap: "learning scope" is reversed — High is good.** Big Bang scores **Low** because there is no *later* wave to apply lessons to; Rollout scores **High** precisely because it is staged.

**Also note:** Big Bang Modular is still **High risk** despite fewer modules, because it still hits **all locations at once** — location count drives risk more than module count does.

items.q: What are the possible **different types of ERP projects**? Why do different projects need different methodologies?
items.answer:
**Not all ERP projects are similar!** Sorted by *what already exists*:

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **First time implementation** | greenfield — no ERP exists |
| **ERP Upgrade** | **obsolescence** or **new version functionality** |
| **Global roll-out** | **global template but country-specific enhancements** |
| **Migration** | **unhappy with current, OR no longer supported** |
| **Harmonization / Consolidation** | **reducing many instances / types of ERPs to one** |
| **Support / Sustain** | ongoing operation |

**Why methodologies must differ** — the work involved is genuinely different:

| Project | As-Is modelling | BPR | Change mgmt | Data conversion | Regression testing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **First-time** | Heavy | Heavy | Heavy | Medium | Low |
| **Upgrade** | **None** | Low | Low | Low | **Heavy** |
| **Migration** | Medium | Medium | Medium | **Heavy** | Medium |
| **Consolidation** | Heavy | Heavy | Heavy | Heavy | Medium |

A methodology built for a greenfield implementation spends months on **As-Is modelling** — **entirely wasted on an upgrade**, where the as-is *is* the system you already run. Conversely an upgrade's emphasis on **regression testing** is barely relevant to a new build.

*This list is also the **emerging trend**: migration, consolidation and upgrades are growing because most large enterprises already own an ERP.*

items.q: What are the **direct** and **indirect** costs of ERP implementation? Explain each.
items.answer:
**The test: does an invoice arrive?** Direct costs have one; indirect costs do not — which is why they are *hidden costs that "come as a surprise"*.

**DIRECT COSTS (9)** — grouped as **Iron, Software, People, Overhead**:

| Bucket | Items |
|---|---|
| **Iron** | **Hardware** (high-end servers, networking, **development setup**, backup system — sized on **users, transactions, reliability, locations**) · **OS and DB** (business-class, special licensing) |
| **Software** | **Application licence fee** (priced **per user by user type**) · **Application maintenance (AMC)** · **Complimentary software** (analytics, office extensions, backup, document management) |
| **People** | **Consulting service** · **Post-implementation support** · **Training** (multi-location, travel) |
| **Overhead** | **PMO cost** |

**INDIRECT COSTS (2) — "People and Pause":**
- **Internal employee cost** — employees **not part of the implementation team**, whose time goes on providing requirements, reviews and acceptance testing. Invisible to the project budget because nobody bills for it.
- **Operational disruption cost** — loss of productivity during changeover.
- Plus **opportunity costs** — the value of what those people and that money would otherwise have produced. The deck itself writes it with a question mark, acknowledging it resists measurement.

**From the sample table (1,914 lakhs total):** the top three lines — **consulting 800, AMC 280, licence 269** — are **70% of the total, and none is hardware.** **AMC (280) exceeds the licence fee (269)**: the recurring cost of owning outgrows the cost of buying.

items.q: What are the **direct (tangible)** and **intangible** benefits of ERP implementation? How does ERP help with **(a) inventory reduction (b) better customer service (c) material and labour cost reduction (d) reduction in days outstanding**?
items.answer:
**TANGIBLE / DIRECT BENEFITS — mnemonic I-C-O-M ("I COMe out ahead"):**

**(a) Inventory reduction** — better management of stock **at different locations and quantities** · handle **expiry-dated/perishable** items · manage **slow-moving/dead stock** · manage availability **based on BOM** · control stock levels **based on orders/forecasting**.

**(b) Better customer service and reduced lost sales** — **minimize lost orders** · **availability in full/part check, no wrong promise** · maintain **min stock levels**, avoiding stock-outs · **quicker planning for short demand surges**.

**(c) Material and labour cost reduction** — **consolidated requirements** to help volume transactions · better vendor supply schedule, **no emergency costs** · forecasts support **buying at the best times** · **less overtime, less idle time** · adjust capacity & schedules.

**(d) Reducing days outstanding** — **accurate and timely invoicing → fewer disputes** · tracking of due and overdue invoices, **reminders, "dunning"** · **link up with order entry** to manage defaulting customers · reduces **currency fluctuation risk** in cross-border transactions. *Days outstanding is a measure of business health and appears in statutory reports.*

**INTANGIBLE BENEFITS:** easy data entry · **information readily available wherever, whenever, to whoever** · **best practices** from the package · quicker operations (quote-to-cash) · **staff morale** · inter-org collaboration · intra-org communication · better data management · improved customer service. *Also: increased turnover, better corporate image, lower risk on money matters.*

**Key insight:** three of the four tangible benefits release **working capital** rather than adding profit — **ERP's financial case is largely a working-capital case**.

**The twist worth adding:** *when ERP is **mandated by a customer**, an intangible benefit becomes entirely tangible* — its value equals the value of the account.

items.q: Build a **business case / ROI analysis** for an ERP implementation. Work through the computation for a company with Rs. 2,000 Cr turnover and an ERP cost of Rs. 19.14 Cr.
items.answer:
**Why the business case is hard:** *"It is easier to calculate **cost** for ERP, as the same can be estimated quickly with estimates from different vendors. **Benefit calculation is always a challenge**, as this is generally based on lots of assumptions and benefits could be intangible and long term."* — a precise number on one side, an estimate on the other.

**Parameters, rationale and extent:**

| Parameter | Rationale | Extent |
|---|---|---|
| **Labor cost saving** | remove/re-organize activities; same person can do more | **2%** |
| **Material cost saving** | better negotiated purchase; focus on high-cost material; economies of scale; **JIT** forecasting | **1%** |
| **Finance cost** | reduced inventory cost; synchronization across stages | **interest @ 12%** |
| **Debtors** | track regularly — **dunning** | **50 → 45 days** |

**The computation:**

1. **Labour:** 2% of 200 Cr → **4 Cr**
2. **Material:** 1% of 1,000 Cr → **1 Cr**
3. **Inventory / finance:** turnover **5 → 6**; value at 5 turns = **400 Cr**, at 6 turns = **333 Cr**; reduction **67 Cr**; @12% → **8 Cr**
4. **Debt management:** working capital **68.4 → 54.79**; interest on the saved **13.6 @ 12%** → **1.62 Cr**

**Total = 4 + 1 + 8 + 1.62 = 23.62 Crore per year**, against a cost of **19.14 Cr over 6 years**.

**The largest single benefit is item 3 — and note it is not a saving on inventory itself but the *interest no longer paid* on the capital that was tied up in it.**

**Two cautions for full marks:**
- **Delayed payback:** *average ROI in the first year could be as little as **5%**; ROI takes **3 years** for most (Meta Group)* — while **Year 1 costs are 1,294 of 1,914 lakhs (68%)**. **Costs peak in Year 1; benefits peak from Year 3.**
- **Track the case:** *"though cost benefit analysis is done in the beginning, actuals might differ — need to track it at the right milestones"*, ploughing the learning back during the support phase.

items.q: Discuss a real ERP implementation — its objectives, what went wrong, the outcome, and the lessons learned.
items.answer:
**NESTLÉ USA — Project BEST (SAP, 1997–2001, $210M)**

*Problem:* after the 1991 reorganisation, divisions remained geographically dispersed — **29 different prices for vanilla to the same vendor**, **nine general ledgers and 28 points of customer entry**, and *"years of autonomous operation provided an almost insurmountable hurdle."* Nestlé was *"the world's No. 1 food and beverage company — but one of the least efficient."*

*Objectives — "One Nestlé, under SAP":* transform separate brands into **one highly integrated company** · establish a **common business process architecture** · **standardize master data**.

*What went wrong:* **the new business process confused most employees, then resistance grew into rebellion in 2000.** Reconstructed June 2000, completed 2001.

*Outcome:* more trustworthy demand forecast · forecasting **down to redistribution-centre level** · **forecast accuracy improved by 2%** · higher factory utilization · reduced inventory · **$371 million saved by 2001** against a $210M budget. **A troubled project with a positive return.**

*Lessons — **DUKE**:* **D**on't start with a **deadline** in mind · **U**pdate your budget projection at regular intervals · **E**RP isn't only about the software · **K**eep communication lines open.

**AGILENT — Project Everest (Oracle E-Business Suite, 2000–2004, $220M)**

*Objectives:* **"One IT"** organization · supply chain capability · migrating **2,200 legacy applications** inherited from HP.

*What went wrong:* consolidating **2,200 systems to under 20**, *"confusion meant lost orders and revenue"* — **$88M reduction in Q3 orders** (of which **$38M lost**, $50M delayed), **$105M lost revenue**, **$70M operating profit**, plus **$35M extra costs**. Root cause: **converting backlog** from legacy systems, *"especially for our highly configured products."*

*Lessons:* implementations are **a lot more than software packages**; **people, processes, policies and culture** all matter; **"ERP disasters are often caused by a user company itself"**; study ERP well before implementation.

**The common conclusion:** two companies, two vendors, two decades — **the same lesson**. Nestlé: *"No major software implementation is really about the software."* Agilent: *"People, processes, policies and culture are all factors."* This is the empirical proof that **ERP is a socio-technical system**.
